1: Open with a question: how many of you have worked a role for two weeks and then found out it was never going to be filled? That time is the cost of poor qualification. This session is about protecting your most valuable asset, which is your time. By the end everyone should be able to qualify a role on one call, grade it A, B or C, and turn the spec into a search plan.
2: Walk through the three outcomes. Check that everyone has brought a live job spec: it gets graded and turned into a search plan later in the session. Timing: 5 minutes.
3: Open with a show of hands: who has spent two weeks on a role that went nowhere? Then ask what they would have needed to know on day one to avoid it. The answer is almost always one of the four questions at the bottom. A strong spec creates clarity, improves search accuracy, saves time, raises candidate quality, manages client expectations and increases fill rates. A weak one does the opposite. The spec is the blueprint for sourcing, outreach and assessment, so this is where every placement starts. Timing: 5 minutes.
4: The original list of questions was a scatter; grouping them into Need, Process, Package and Risk makes them easy to remember and easy to check off on the call. Need tells you how to sell the role (a backfill, a growth hire and a restructure sound very different to a candidate). Process tells you how fast you can move and who you really need to influence. Package tells you whether the role is fillable in today’s market. Risk tells you how much of your time it deserves. Ask the room which column they most often skip: usually Risk. Timing: 8 minutes.
5: A high-quality job has a strong probability of being filled, a committed client and clear requirements. Ask each person to hold up their live spec and score it against the six cards, one point each. Anything under four is a warning sign: either qualify it further with the client this week or deprioritise it. The core rule in lime is the short version to remember on the desk. Timing: 6 minutes.
6: Most job descriptions list fifteen requirements as if they were all equal. In reality three to five are non-negotiable and the rest are a wish list. Every nice-to-have you can move out of the must-have column widens the talent pool. The test question is the most useful single question in this module: say it word for word on every qualification call. Then ask the three follow-ups: top non-negotiables, where they could flex for an exceptional candidate, and what made previous hires successful. Note on work authorisation: it is a fair must-have to confirm, but ask it as “authorised to work in the US” and “need sponsorship now or in future”, not about citizenship or visa type. Timing: 7 minutes.
7: Grading is how you protect your time. A jobs get your best hours and your best candidates. B jobs get worked steadily, with a plan to turn them into A jobs (ask for exclusivity once you have proven quality). C jobs get minimal time; the right move is often to go back to the client and ask what it would take to make it exclusive, or to walk away. Ask everyone to grade their live spec now using the five quick questions and say the grade out loud. Then ask: what would it take to move it up one grade? Timing: 8 minutes.
8: The qualification call gives you everything you need here. If you can’t fill in all three cards, the role isn’t qualified yet; go back to the client. Ask someone to build a persona live for a role on their desk and have the room challenge it: is the company list too narrow? Are we only fishing in the obvious ponds? Ten minutes.
9: Build the string live on LinkedIn Recruiter with the group and show how results change as you add or remove an AND. Common mistake: putting nice-to-haves in the AND chain and shrinking the pool to nothing. Keep nice-to-haves out of the string and use them to rank the results instead. Run the same logic across channels: LinkedIn, the CRM, job boards, GitHub for engineers. Throughout the search, feed market feedback back to the client and requalify the role if priorities change.
10: Use real roles from the floor so the output is useful straight away. The “hiring manager” should hold back information unless asked the right question; that is the point of the drill. In the debrief, ask two pairs to read out their grade and string. Did anyone downgrade a role once they asked the right questions? That’s the lesson.
11: Close on the principle: spend your time on the jobs that are qualified, the clients who are engaged and the searches most likely to fill. Ask each person to write down their three takeaways and the first action they’ll take. Managers: review everyone’s A/B/C grades in the next pipeline meeting.
12: Open the floor for questions. Point to Module 05: the best way to get more A jobs is to win them through business development.
